subject: Mathematics
title: Number Bases
content:
A number base tells how many digits a counting system uses. Base 10 (decimal) uses 0–9; base 2 (binary) uses 0 and 1; base 8 (octal) 0–7; base 16 (hexadecimal) 0–9, A–F.

Convert base 10 → other base: repeated division, read remainders upwards. E.g. 45 in base 2: 45÷2=22 r1, 22÷2=11 r0, 11÷2=5 r1, 5÷2=2 r1, 2÷2=1 r0, 1÷2=0 r1 → 101101₂.

Other base → base 10: expand in powers. 1011₂ = 1×2³ + 0×2² + 1×2¹ + 1×2⁰ = 8+0+2+1 = 11.

Addition/subtraction/multiplication are done in the given base with carries in that base.
keyPoints: Binary digits: 0, 1 only
Repeated division to convert OUT of base 10
Powers expansion to convert INTO base 10

subject: Mathematics
title: Indices and Standard Form
content:
Laws of indices: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a.

Standard form: A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10. E.g. 45,000 = 4.5 × 10⁴; 0.00072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁴.

Multiplying standard forms: multiply the A's, add the powers. Dividing: divide A's, subtract powers. (4.5×10⁴)(2×10²) = 9×10⁶.
keyPoints: a⁰ = 1; negative index = reciprocal
Standard form: A × 10ⁿ, 1 ≤ A < 10
Add powers when multiplying, subtract when dividing

subject: Mathematics
title: Logarithms
content:
Logarithm answers the question: what power gives this number? log₂8 = 3 because 2³ = 8.

Laws: log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a − log b; log aⁿ = n log a; log₁₀1 = 0; log₁₀10 = 1.

Use log tables or calculators to simplify hard multiplication/division: convert to logs, add/subtract, convert back with antilog.

Worked example: 240 × 0.035: log 240 = 2.3802, log 0.035 = 2.5441 (i.e. −1.4559). Sum = 0.9243 → antilog ≈ 8.4.
keyPoints: log(ab) = log a + log b — turns × into +
log(a/b) = log a − log b — turns ÷ into −
log aⁿ = n log a — brings powers down

subject: Mathematics
title: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
A set is a well-defined collection. Notation: ∈ (member), ⊂ (subset), ∪ (union, OR), ∩ (intersection, AND), n(A) = number of members, A′ = complement.

Venn diagram problems with two sets: n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B).

Worked example: In a class, 20 like Physics, 15 like Chemistry, 8 like both. How many like at least one? n(P∪C) = 20 + 15 − 8 = 27.
keyPoints: Union = OR, intersection = AND
n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B)
For three sets use the 8-region Venn diagram

subject: Mathematics
title: Linear Equations
content:
A linear equation has the unknown to power 1. Solve by balancing: do the same to both sides.

Example: 3x + 5 = 20 → 3x = 15 → x = 5.
With brackets: 2(x − 3) = 10 → 2x − 6 = 10 → x = 8.
With fractions: multiply everything by the LCM first.

Word problems: define the unknown, form the equation, solve, CHECK against the story.
keyPoints: Balance both sides — same operation each side
Expand brackets and clear fractions first
Always check your solution in the original equation

subject: Mathematics
title: Simultaneous Equations
content:
Two unknowns, two equations. Methods:
• Elimination: make one variable's coefficients equal, add/subtract.
• Substitution: express one variable from one equation, substitute into the other.

Example: x + y = 10; x − y = 2. Add: 2x = 12, x = 6, then y = 4.

Graphical method: plot both lines; the intersection point is the solution. Word problems (ages, prices) translate directly into two equations.
keyPoints: Elimination: add when signs differ, subtract when same
Substitution: isolate, then substitute
Solution satisfies BOTH equations — always verify

subject: Mathematics
title: Quadratic Equations
content:
Form: ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0). Four solution methods:
1. Factorisation: x² + 5x + 6 = 0 → (x+2)(x+3) = 0 → x = −2 or −3
2. Completing the square: x² + bx → (x + b/2)² − (b/2)²
3. Formula: x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a — works always
4. Graph: roots are where the curve cuts the x-axis.

The discriminant b² − 4ac tells the root type: >0 two real roots, =0 equal roots, <0 no real roots.
keyPoints: Standard form ax² + bx + c = 0
Formula: x = [−b ± √(b²−4ac)]/2a
b²−4ac decides the nature of roots

subject: Mathematics
title: Geometry — Lines, Angles and Triangles
content:
Angle facts: angles on a straight line = 180°; vertically opposite angles are equal; angles at a point = 360°; corresponding & alternate angles are equal (parallel lines + transversal).

Triangles: angle sum = 180°. Types by sides (equilateral 60° each, isosceles 2 equal, scalene) and angles (acute, right, obtuse).

Exterior angle of a triangle = sum of the two opposite interior angles. Polygon angle sum = (n−2)×180°.
keyPoints: Straight line = 180°; point = 360°
Triangle angles = 180°; exterior angle rule
Polygon sum = (n−2)×180°

subject: Mathematics
title: Trigonometry — Introduction
content:
In a right-angled triangle, for angle θ:
• SOH: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse
• CAH: cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse
• TOA: tan θ = opposite/adjacent

Special angles: sin 30° = 0.5, sin 45° = 0.7071, sin 60° = 0.8661; cos 60° = 0.5; tan 45° = 1.

Use to find heights and distances: the angle of elevation is measured UP from the horizontal, depression DOWN.

Example: a ladder 10 m leans on a wall at 60° to the ground. Height reached = 10 sin 60° = 8.66 m.
keyPoints: SOH CAH TOA
Angle of elevation up, depression down
Label sides before choosing the ratio
